newsitem.title: UK: Russia fuel exports fall to 700-850 kt in January.
newsitem.headline: Russia fuel exports fall to 700-850 kt in January.

text.p: Russia's heavy fuel oil exports from the Baltics and the Black Sea have fallen to about 750-850,000 tonnes in January, about half a million tonnes down from December, but were roughly double last year's levels, traders and brokers said.

Fuel oil exports to Europe from the Baltic ports of Klaipeda, Ventspils, Tallinn and St.Petersburg were assessed at 500-600,000 tonnes in January, compared to 900,000 tonnes in both December and November.

Exports from the Baltics last January were assessed at just a quarter of a million tonnes and dealers attributed this year's dramatic rise largely to the Russian governments failure this year to repeat the export ban that had been imposed in previous winters.
Exports from the Black Sea were assessed at around 200-250,000 tonnes in January.

Figures for December were not immediately available but one dealer said he thought exports may have been as much as 400,000 tonnes. Comparative figures for last year were not available but traders said they were lower than this year.
High sulphur fuel oil prices in Europe are currently around 70 percent of the value of crude oil, compared with over 85 percent at the end of January last year.
Dealers attribute this weakness as much to the increased Russian export volumes as to a longer-term slowdown in European demand.

Traders were also expecting late last year that Russia would impose an increased export tariff on fuel oil, or mazut, this winter. Such a tariff increase has failed to materialise, although the railways ministry said this month they had boosted internal rail freight rates for refined oil products by around 15 percent.

Traders are generally wary of predicting Russian export patterns. But they feel that export levels are unlikely to fluctuate as wildly as in previous years, as local traders become more accustomed to market economics and boost their exports during the winter, when prices are high.
Fuel oil prices are also weak relative to crude oil because of a long term decline in demand, especially from Italy's state power company ENEL, the world's largest single buyer of fuel oil.
Italian industry sources see fuel oil in Italy being rapidly displaced by natural gas, whose use is expected to rise by 10 percent a year from now until 2000.
